problems: MINOR DOC INACCURACY (does not change outcome): the watermark is font-size:46px font-weight:700 = 34.5pt bold, which is WCAG 'large text', so the applicable 1.4.3 threshold is 3:1, NOT the 4.5:1 stated in case-01.md (lines 33-34) and the HTML comment (line 112). The text still fails the correct 3:1 large-text threshold at 1.56:1, so the 'failed' outcome stands, but the rationale cites the wrong required ratio.
The .md and HTML comment repeatedly assert 'must meet 4.5:1'; for this large bold text the precise requirement is 3:1. Recommend correcting the threshold wording for accuracy, not dropping the case.

Cosmetic prompt/page drift: the orchestration prompt describes the flourish as 'INSPIRE' at '35% alpha', but the actual HTML (line 83) and the .md both use the word 'WANDER' at color rgba(255,255,255,.30) (30% alpha). The HTML and .md are internally consistent; only the prompt's framing string is stale. Not a page defect.

The 'tools false-positive' narrative is partially overstated for axe-core specifically: axe-core SKIPS aria-hidden=true text for color-contrast and would therefore pass silently rather than raise a false positive. The doc hedges adequately ('or report needs-review when sampling over the photo') and the cited trusted-tester ANDI/CCA manual flow WOULD surface the faint word as a 'Manual Contrast Test Needed', so the human-judgment value (ruling it exempt) still holds. Worth a one-line tightening but not disqualifying.

Computed contrast of the flourish over the brightest scene pixel (#c9cdbf) is ~1.17:1, slightly below the doc's stated '1.4-2.0:1' floor; this only strengthens the 'fails if in scope' claim, so it is a precision nit not an error.

Borderline automated-detectability: a plain ratio checker (axe-core) does NOT exempt large text from contrast checks — it applies the 3:1 large-text bar, and 2.52 < 3, so axe WOULD already flag this element as a contrast violation. The genuinely human-only part is the decorative-vs-informative SCOPE judgment, not the ratio itself; the failing ratio is mechanically catchable, which weakens the 'tools miss it' framing in the .md (lines 37-44) and HTML comment (lines 90-100).

Minor: the .md/HTML comment claim that scanners 'down-weight large text' and therefore miss it is misleading — mainstream scanners apply the 3:1 large-text threshold and still fail 2.52:1; they would not silently pass it.

Minor framing weakness (not a defect): the divider is aria-hidden="true", and the strongest contrast checker (axe-core's color-contrast rule) excludes elements hidden from AT, so axe would already correctly NOT fail this page. The doc's 'tools false-positive' claim only holds for naive ratio scanners that read visible text and ignore aria-hidden; the genuine human-judgment content is distinguishing this decorative repeated word from a meaningful one (the case-01 pair), not merely computing 1.5:1.

The .md attribute tuple references case-01 as 'DRAFT' (the meaningful repeated-word counterpart); I did not verify case-01 exists/has the opposite ruling, so the claimed structural-pair contrast is asserted but unverified here.

PROMPT/HARNESS METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): the prompt's claimed scenario describes a 'patient-intake multi-step form' with an '01 02 03' step rail, selector '.step.current .ord', #d0d0d0=1.54:1, citing the decoration-exemption for a step indicator. The ACTUAL file (case-05.html) is a transit ticket whose meaningful text is platform code 'B7' (.platform .code), color #c8cdca over an inline-SVG floorplan image. The prompt's selector '.step.current .ord' does NOT exist in the file (querySelector returns null; inspect.js fell back to RootWebArea). Citation file in the prompt (refs/trusted-tester/sc-1.4.3-contrast-minimum.md) differs from the citation in case-05.md (WCAG Understanding contrast-minimum.html). Both quotes are legitimately verbatim in their respective sources — the trusted-tester quote 'Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)' is verbatim at line 12 — but the cross-file citation inconsistency is worth flagging.

Secondary/out-of-scope defect on the same element: .platform has role='img' aria-label='Station floorplan with platform code' which does NOT contain 'B7', and the .code span resolves to ax role=none — so the sole platform cue is entirely absent from the accessibility tree for screen-reader users. This is a real 1.1.1/1.3.1 issue but does not affect the 1.4.3 visual-contrast verdict (1.4.3 concerns visual presentation, and the glyph is visibly rendered).

Minor (not disqualifying): the page's PASS hinges entirely on the evaluator recognizing the string 'acmecorp.com' as THE registered company wordmark, but the source provides no independent proof of brand status (no logo, no registered-mark glyph, only the aria-label and a code comment). This is the intended human-judgment hook, but a strict reviewer must take the 'this is a logotype' premise on the page's word.

The aria-label='Acmecorp' drops the '.com' TLD that is visually rendered; AT users get 'Acmecorp' while sighted users see 'acmecorp.com'. Harmless for a brand mark and not a 1.4.3 concern, but a minor name/visual mismatch worth noting.

The measured 2.07:1 fails both, so the 'failed' outcome is correct regardless, but the cited threshold is technically wrong for this size/weight.

Partial automated detectability: a stock contrast scanner (axe/Lighthouse/WAVE) DOES compute and flag 2.07:1 on this text node (the page itself admits this, HTML lines 73-85). The human judgment is required to UPHOLD the flag against the 'logos are exempt' defense, not to FIND the low contrast. So the element is not invisible to tooling; the dispositive reasoning (exemption erosion via UI-component function) is the human part.

The case is legitimately human-judgment-dependent in that framing, but it is not a case an automated tool would MISS (it would over-flag, not under-flag).

That distinction is genuinely non-automatable, but the doc's framing that tools 'miss' the failure overstates it — tools over-flag here and would happen to be correct.

This is an intentional PASS/exempt boundary case, not a failure — so there is no real accessibility error (by design). errorIsReal=false reflects 'no genuine SC 1.4.3 violation', which is correct for the page's intent.

SELF-REFUTING CITATION (decisive): the page cites WCAG Understanding 1.4.3 VERBATIM (confirmed at contrast-minimum.html lines 75-77): 'refer to the foreground and background colors obtained from the user agent, or the underlying markup and stylesheets, RATHER THAN the text as presented on screen.' A defensible narrow reading exists (the note targets author-uncontrollable anti-aliasing; mix-blend-mode is author CSS), so it is contested — but the page quotes as SUPPORT an authority whose plain text points the other way.

F24 MISATTRIBUTION: the F24 quote at failures/F24.html line 86 is verbatim-accurate, but F24's Expected Results (lines 95-96) make the failure apply only when a foreground is specified WITHOUT a background (or vice versa). The cited cascade sentence is a side-note, not the failure mechanism — wrong failure technique for a both-colors-present blend case.

CONTESTED NORMATIVE BASIS: whether SC 1.4.3 is judged on declared CSSOM colors (8.3:1 pass) or composited rendered pixels (1.46:1 fail) is genuinely debatable; the 'failed' label is not cleanly correct under the page's own cited normative text.

An axe-style checker that flattens rgba against an assumed-white page background may surface this as a violation or 'incomplete' rather than truly missing it; the human-judgment value rests on the fact that axe abstains (incomplete) on multi-layer/backdrop-filter composites rather than the value being a clean pass-under-naive-tooling.
The doc/scenario states ~2.2:1; my composite computation gives 2.24:1 over the white page area and 2.17:1 over the banner region — consistent with the claim (minor rounding only, not a defect).

None material. The accessible name of .hero h1 is fully correct (Book Your Sunset Escape, heading level 1) and intentional: the failure is purely perceptual (sighted low-vision contrast), not an AT-name defect, which is precisely why name/role checkers and the AX tree cannot detect it.
